title: Mountain Doctrine: Ocean of Definitive Meaning (ri chos nges don rgya mtsho)
alt_titles: ri chos nges don rgya mtsho zhes bya ba mthar thug thun mong ma yin pa'i man ngag

structure.description: organized, as recalled, around the ground (buddha-nature as the ultimate), the path and the fruit; heavily built of scriptural citation (structure: low confidence)

editions.name: J. Hopkins, Mountain Doctrine: Tibet's Fundamental Treatise on Other-Emptiness and the Buddha-Matrix (2006)

notes: Not found in the local catalogue (search 'Mountain Doctrine', 'ri chos nges don rgya mtsho' returned only unrelated works); existence and authorship are well known.
summary: Dolpopa's principal treatise on other-emptiness, written as final, uncommon instructions for mountain retreatants. It sets out buddha-nature (the matrix of the one gone thus) as the ultimate that is empty of all adventitious, conventional phenomena but not of its own nature, permanent and endowed with the buddha-qualities; distinguishes self-emptiness of the conventional from other-emptiness of the ultimate; and supports this with extensive citation of the tathāgatagarbha sūtras, the Maitreya texts, Nāgārjuna's hymns and the Kālacakra literature.

title: The Great Calculation of the Doctrine which has the Significance of a Fourth Council (bka' bsdu bzhi pa'i don bstan rtsis chen po)
alt_titles: The Great Calculation of the Doctrine

editions.name: English translations by C. Stearns (The Buddha from Dolpo) and J. Hopkins (as recalled)

summary: Dolpopa's short verse work (with his own commentary) presenting his teaching as a 'fourth council': it reckons the ages of the doctrine and holds that the teaching of the age of perfection (kṛtayuga), preserved in the Kālacakra and the definitive sūtras, is the Buddha's final intent — the ultimate empty of other.

title: A General Commentary on the Doctrine (bstan pa spyi 'grel)

editions.name: C. Stearns, The Buddha from Dolpo (as recalled)

summary: A short work by Dolpopa, in the form of a supplication, summarizing his whole understanding of the doctrine — the two truths as self-empty and other-empty, the definitive sūtras and tantras, and the path of the vajra-yoga.

title: The Essence of Other-Emptiness (gzhan stong snying po)

editions.name: J. Hopkins, The Essence of Other-Emptiness (2007)

summary: Tāranātha's concise presentation of the other-emptiness view: the three natures (imputational, other-powered, thoroughly established), the two truths, the difference between self-emptiness and other-emptiness, and the thoroughly established nature as self-aware primordial wisdom, empty of what is other than it.

title: Twenty-one Differences regarding the Profound Meaning (zab don khyad par nyer gcig pa)
summary: Tāranātha's list of twenty-one points on which the other-emptiness (shentong) Madhyamaka differs from the self-emptiness (rangtong) Madhyamaka — on the two truths, the three natures, buddha-nature, the qualities, and what is established in meditative equipoise.

title: The Ornament of Other-Emptiness Madhyamaka (gzhan stong dbu ma'i rgyan)
summary: A work of Tāranātha setting out other-emptiness as the Great Madhyamaka and answering objections (content not recalled in detail).

structure.description: four tantras: Root (6 chapters), Explanatory (31), Oral Instruction (92), Subsequent (27, i.e. 25 plus 2 concluding); 156 chapters in all

editions.name: English translations of parts (e.g. Men-Tsee-Khang; Clark, The Quintessence Tantras of Tibetan Medicine)

notes: Chapter counts per tantra: high confidence for 6/31/92; the Subsequent Tantra counted as 27 (25+2) — moderate.
summary: The root text of Tibetan medicine, in four tantras and 156 chapters, framed as a dialogue in which the sage Rigpé Yeshe (the Medicine Buddha's mind-emanation) answers Yilé Kyé: the Root Tantra gives the whole system as three trees; the Explanatory Tantra covers embryology, anatomy, physiology, the causes and classes of disease, conduct, diet, pharmacology, diagnosis, treatment principles and the physician; the Oral Instruction Tantra treats the diseases one by one; the Subsequent Tantra gives pulse and urine diagnosis, the preparation of medicines and the evacuative and external therapies.

title: The Root Tantra (rtsa rgyud) of the Four Tantras

tradition.text: the word of the Medicine Buddha, translated in the 8th c. by Vairocana, hidden at Samye and recovered as treasure by Drapa Ngönshé in 1038

scholarly.text: compiled in the 12th c. by Yuthok Yönten Gönpo the Younger, drawing on the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya and other sources

summary: Six chapters: the setting in the medicine city Tanaduk; the request; the basis (health and disease: the three nyepa, seven constituents, three excretions); diagnosis (seeing, touching, questioning); treatment (diet, behaviour, medicine, external therapy); and the summary of all by the image of three trees.

title: The Explanatory Tantra (bshad rgyud) of the Four Tantras

structure.description: 31 chapters (individual chapter numbers used in teachings are low-confidence)

summary: Thirty-one chapters explaining the basis in detail: embryology, the similes, anatomy (channels, vital points), physiology, the classes of the body, the signs of death, the causes, conditions, onset, characteristics and classes of disease, daily, seasonal and occasional conduct, diet and its restrictions, the tastes and potencies of medicines, instruments, health preservation, diagnosis, treatment principles, and the qualities of the physician.

title: The Oral Instruction Tantra (man ngag rgyud) of the Four Tantras

tradition.text: the word of the Medicine Buddha, translated in the 8th c. by Vairocana, hidden at Samye and recovered as treasure by Drapa Ngönshé in 1038

scholarly.text: compiled in the 12th c. by Yuthok Yönten Gönpo the Younger, drawing on the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya and other sources

summary: Ninety-two chapters on the treatment of particular diseases: disorders of the three nyepa, internal diseases, fevers, diseases of the upper body and organs, diseases of the private parts, miscellaneous and spreading diseases, children's and women's diseases, spirit (gdon) afflictions, wounds, poisons, and the rejuvenation (bcud len) and virility chapters.

title: The Subsequent Tantra (phyi ma rgyud) of the Four Tantras

tradition.text: the word of the Medicine Buddha, translated in the 8th c. by Vairocana, hidden at Samye and recovered as treasure by Drapa Ngönshé in 1038

scholarly.text: compiled in the 12th c. by Yuthok Yönten Gönpo the Younger, drawing on the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya and other sources

summary: The last tantra: pulse diagnosis (ch. 1) and urine diagnosis (ch. 2), the pacifying medicines (decoctions, powders, pills, pastes, medicinal butters, calcined preparations, concentrates, medicinal wines, jewel medicines, herbal compounds), the evacuative therapies, the gentle and rough external therapies, and the concluding chapters on entrusting the teaching.
